    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">As our flexible electricity use lead <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/brian-fitzgerald-6b9ba296?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Brian Fitzgerald</a> told the HVAC&R conference yesterday, harnessing flexibility could save the country billions in energy costs, and data centres are an important part of harnessing that potential.

Brian was talking flex at Auckland showgrounds at New Zealand’s largest trade-only event for the heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration sector.

Our Energy End Use Database shows data centres' energy demands are growing rapidly – a trend that is likely to continue.

While data centres account for only at 0.6% of final national electricity demand currently, due to our proportion of renewable electricity, stable regulatory environment and cooler ambient temperatures, New Zealand is seen as a strong potential contender for international investors looking for suitable data centre sites.

Advanced cooling methods will matter hugely when it comes to making data centres the most efficient and flexible energy users they can be.

As hyperscale data centres continue to be a hot button topic around the world, EECA is standing up research to ensure we understand the opportunities and challenges data centres bring from both an efficiency and flexibility perspective - and to ensure we learn from international best practice.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We’re pleased to welcome a new Chair and three new Board members to the EECA Board.

Together, they bring a strong mix of expertise, networks and experience across energy and infrastructure, demand-side management, sustainability, regulatory governance and more. We look forward to working with them as we continue to deliver value across the energy system.

We also acknowledge and thank outgoing Board members Dr <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/dtulloch?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Daniel Tulloch</a>, <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/christopher-boyle-94964534?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Christopher Boyle</a> and <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/judi-jones-ombudsman?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Judi Jones</a>, whose terms have come to a close.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">What role could future fuels play in New Zealand's energy system?

From aviation and shipping to forestry and agriculture, many sectors may require alternatives to fossil fuels.

EECA has launched a new RFP seeking expert research partners to help build a stronger evidence base on future fuels like sustainable aviation fuel, hydrogen, and green ammonia in New Zealand. 

The research will explore technology developments, production pathways, potential use cases, economics, feedstock requirements and scalability across different scenarios. 

This work will help improve understanding of:
➡️ how the economics of different fuels may evolve over time.
➡️ where feedstocks and raw materials could be sourced.
➡️ the infrastructure and energy requirements associated with different pathways.
➡️ what scale-up opportunities and challenges may emerge.

We are looking for organisations with expertise in energy systems, market analysis, modelling, and strategic research to help shape this important piece of work.

Proposals close: 22 July 2026

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We recently joined the Hawke’s Bay Chamber of Commerce’s inaugural energy summit, where more than 200 business leaders came together to discuss the region’s energy future and the importance of planning ahead.

While the region isn’t one of the country’s largest energy consumers, it is among the most impacted by changes in gas supply. Take aways from the day include: 

➡️ Food processing, manufacturing, forestry and other industries that depend on process heat are key to the Hawke's Bay economy - making forward planning important. The businesses that look ahead will be better positioned to manage challenges and take advantage of emerging opportunities.
➡️ For a region with a strong forestry and wood processing sector, biomass represents a significant opportunity to improve energy resilience and reduce emissions.
➡️ Energy is one of the most important issues facing many businesses, and continued collaboration will be key to ensuring the region remains resilient and competitive in the years ahead.

A huge thank you to the Hawke’s Bay Chamber of Commerce and everyone who contributed to the conversation. We're looking for experienced organisations to help build a robust, evidence-based understanding of organic waste feedstocks in Northland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Wellington, and Manawatū-Whanganui. The work will assess feedstock availability, location, seasonality, and renewable energy potential, with a particular focus on anaerobic digestion and biogas opportunities.
